design_detail: Exploratory systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; no registered protocol) of psychological changes and adverse effects from 1 day to 1 month after classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT, 5-MeO-DMT, mescaline, ayahuasca) in adults, from studies of any design that measured outcomes with standardized published instruments before and after use. MEDLINE and Web of Science searched from 1950 to 17 August 2021, English and German. 48 studies (52 publications), 1774 participants; results summarized by counting studies reporting a statistically significant increase, decrease, other change or no change in each of 19 outcome domains.
can_establish: Which psychological changes and adverse effects studies up to August 2021 reported in the month after a classic psychedelic, in which outcome domains changes were reported most consistently, how often adverse after-effects were looked for, and what kinds were reported.
cannot_establish: How large the changes are (no effect sizes or pooling); whether they are caused by the drug rather than expectation, setting, selection or regression to the mean (71% of studies lacked a standardized placebo-controlled double-blind design); how often after-effects occur in recreational use, where preparation and aftercare are usually absent (the authors say the results cannot be generalized there); how often adverse effects occur (only about half the studies said they looked, mostly without standard checklists); and whether post-session support changes the after-effects (the authors state this has not been tested).

sample.recruitment: MEDLINE via PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection to 17 August 2021, plus reference lists; 3973 publications screened after removing duplicates, 1918 excluded on title and abstract and 2003 on full text (Results › Study selection and sample characteristics, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human adults, clinical or nonclinical, any study type with baseline and pre–post analysis of standardized published psychological instruments between 1 day and 1 month after use; all reports of subacute adverse effects in any form. Excluded: studies that ended the acute experience with antipsychotics by default, microdosing, projective tests, book chapters, poster abstracts, case reports, reviews, comments and follow-ups not clearly timed; languages other than English and German.
sample.demographics: Sample sizes 6 to 315 (mean 38, median 18); 7 publications from 1958 to 1971 (86% LSD), none from 1972 to 1998, 45 from 1999 to 2021 (mostly psilocybin or ayahuasca); 35% clinical samples (depression, cancer-related distress, addiction and others), 65% healthy or unselected convenience samples. 83% of studies had at least one follow-up within two weeks.
sample.selection_effects: Laboratory trials and observational studies of ceremonies, both with preparation and aftercare; English and German only; only statistically significant results counted. Observational studies were mostly of ayahuasca (60%) and controlled studies mostly of psilocybin and LSD (86%), so substance and design are confounded.

exposure.measurement: Administration in laboratory or clinical studies, or self-selected use in ceremonies and retreats (observational studies).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated (Table 1): LSD 50 to 450 µg by mouth (one study 75 µg intravenously; one 3 µg/kg); psilocybin 0.143 to 0.4 mg/kg or 10 to 32 mg; ayahuasca by volume with stated DMT content where known; 5-MeO-DMT 17 to 61 mg inhaled; mescaline 0.5 g injected; doses not reported in several observational studies. Mostly single sessions, some with two to six sessions. Follow-up 1 day to 1 month after the session.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; observational ceremony studies did not control other substance use.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: outcomes were measured 1 day to 1 month after a session.

comparison.controls: Each person's own baseline in all studies; a control group in 24 of 48 studies (placebo-controlled and double-blind in 14).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectation, motivation and selection into ceremonies or trials were not assessed; floor effects for anxiety and suicidality in healthy samples are noted by the authors.

outcomes.instruments: Standardized published scales in 19 domains (for example depression, anxiety, mood, wellbeing and life satisfaction, mindfulness, personality and attitudes, social effects, spirituality, creativity, psychosis, mania, cognitive performance, complaints); adverse events in any form reported by the studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: Only standardized and published instruments were accepted, which the authors use as their outcome-level safeguard against bias.
outcomes.operationalization: Each study's result in each domain was coded as increase, decrease, other change or no change according to the statistical significance of pre–post differences (or drug-by-time interactions); trends were ignored.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable; significance as reported by the primary studies.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; most outcomes are self-reports.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Results are counts of studies reporting significant change per domain (Figure 2, an image, and Supplementary Tables S1 to S3, not read). Text figures: changes were most consistent (70 to 90% of studies investigating the domain, more than 450 participants) for depression, stress and grief; mindfulness, acceptance and emotion regulation; personality, values and attitudes; wellbeing and life satisfaction; and social effects. No changes in manic or psychotic symptoms or cognitive performance (few studies). Adverse events: 25 studies (52%, 550 participants) said whether they assessed them; 11 (297 participants) reported none and 14 (253 participants) reported 52 headaches, 6 cases of insomnia or sleep disturbance, 6 of tension, 3 of exhaustion, 3 of visual distortion, 2 each of fatigue, migraine, nausea, difficulty concentrating and vivid dreams, and single cases including severe anxiety exacerbation with relapse to methamphetamine use and a psychiatric disturbance lasting a week.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only statistically significant findings were counted (vote counting), so non-significant results and their direction are lost; the authors discuss possible publication bias and selective reporting in a field with high public interest.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the median study had 18 participants.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 48 mostly small studies, many of them uncontrolled, the changes reported in the month after a classic psychedelic were mostly towards less depression and stress and more wellbeing, mindfulness and social connectedness, with no group-level worsening of psychopathology. Adverse after-effects were reported in 14 of the 25 studies that said they looked: mostly headaches, then sleep problems, tension and exhaustion, with rare severe events.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the results support narrative reports of a subacute afterglow comprising potentially beneficial changes, and that subacute adverse events were mild to severe with no serious adverse events. The authors are careful elsewhere: they state that the findings summarize effects observed under favourable conditions, should not be taken as the average expected effect, and cannot be generalized to recreational use. Remaining gaps: (1) vote counting of significant pre–post changes cannot show that the drug caused them; (2) ‘no serious adverse events’ sits beside a severe anxiety exacerbation with relapse and a week-long psychiatric disturbance, and half the studies did not say whether they looked; (3) the comparison of subacute side effects with those of SSRIs is not based on data.

timeline.event: Pahnke and colleagues' description (JAMA, 1970) of the psychedelic afterglow lasting about two weeks to a month, quoted in this review's introduction.
Müller et al. pooled analysis of flashback phenomena after LSD and psilocybin in six controlled trials, which reports a later-weeks after-effect not covered by this review's outcome domains
This review: the first systematic review restricted to the subacute window, by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic map of subacute effects of psychedelics in the papers read for this card. It shows where changes have been reported, not how large or how causal they are; a meta-analysis cited in its introduction combined subacute with long-term effects and is not separable from it.

what_would_settle_it: Placebo-controlled trials, and prospective studies of people using psychedelics outside research, with daily ratings of mood, sleep, headache and distress over the month after use using a standard adverse-effect checklist and a validated afterglow instrument, reporting effect sizes for both benefits and harms.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are 'no' (2 protocol, 4 search, 7 excluded studies, 9 risk of bias), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. This is partly a consequence of the review's exploratory aim, which the authors state, and their interpretation is cautious. It may be cited for the inventory of studies and outcome domains, for the direction of reported changes as counts of studies, for the list of reported adverse after-effects with the caveat that half the studies did not say whether they looked, and for the authors' statement that the results reflect favourable settings; it should not be cited for the size or causation of any afterglow effect or for its frequency in recreational use.

key_findings.finding: 48 studies (52 publications) with 1774 participants were included: 16 psilocybin, 16 ayahuasca, 10 LSD, 2 5-MeO-DMT, 3 several psychedelics and 1 mescaline; 17 clinical and 31 nonclinical samples; sample sizes 6 to 315 (median 18); follow-up 1 day to 1 month.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study selection and sample characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 2, All studies row

key_findings.finding: 14 of 48 studies (29%) had a standardized treatment with placebo control and double-blind allocation, 19 (40%) a standardized treatment without control or blinding, and 15 (31%) no standardization (observational); controlled studies were mostly of psilocybin and LSD (86%), observational studies mostly of ayahuasca (60%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias, 1st paragraph; Table 2, footnote a

key_findings.finding: Changes were reported most consistently (in 70 to 90% of the studies that measured them, each domain with more than 450 participants) for depression, stress and grief; mindfulness, acceptance and emotion regulation; personality, values and attitudes; wellbeing and life satisfaction; and social effects. Mindfulness data came only from healthy or unselected samples, and mindfulness and wellbeing data mostly from observational studies.

No study reported group-level worsening of psychopathology, and none found increases in suicidality, manic or psychotic symptoms or decreases in cognitive performance, although few studies assessed these outcomes.

Only 25 of 48 studies (52%, 550 participants) said whether they assessed adverse events. Of these, 11 (297 participants) reported none and 14 (253 participants) reported subacute adverse events: 52 headaches (usually lasting no more than a day or two), 6 cases of insomnia or sleep disturbance, 6 of tension, 3 of exhaustion, 3 of visual distortion, 2 each of fatigue, migraine, nausea, difficulty concentrating and vivid dreams, and single cases including severe anxiety exacerbation with relapse to methamphetamine use, a post-traumatic stress flashback with tinnitus and panic, and a psychiatric disturbance lasting a week.
Of four studies that collected complaints with a standardized list, three found no change and one an increase in complaints one day after use that had gone at one week.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Subacute effects of psychedelics, Figure 2 footnote d

key_findings.finding: Most subacute effects were seen in all three follow-up windows, most consistently between 3 and 14 days; results at 1 to 2 days were the most variable; increases in creativity were limited to the early windows.

The authors state that the results come from laboratory studies and ceremonies with preparation and aftercare, cannot be generalized to recreational use, may be biased by selective reporting, and should be read as a summary of effects observed under favourable conditions, not as the average expected effect.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists Dolder et al. (2016) with 243 participants, but the LSD total (362) and the overall total (1774) in Table 2 match the Table 1 rows only if that study contributes no participants (editors' arithmetic: the other LSD studies, counting the repeated Schmid sample once, sum to 362).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the 243 is a misprint or the totals omit that study; the total participant count is uncertain by up to 243.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusion state that no serious adverse events were reported, while the adverse-event list includes a severe anxiety exacerbation with relapse to methamphetamine use and a psychiatric disturbance lasting one week.
reporting_issues.consequence: Depends on the definition of serious; claims should name these events rather than repeat that none was serious.
